小鑼圈為泰國古典音樂使用的體鳴樂器，由十八個帶乳突的調音鑼組成，發聲依靠鑼體振動: The khong wong lek is an idiophone used in Thai classical music, made up of eighteen tuned bossed gongs, sounding through the vibration of the gong bodies. The only material the source records is beeswax, used to tune underneath each gong; it says nothing about the materials of the body, the frame, the beaters or the other parts, so the construction cannot be described in more detail.
小鑼圈音色清亮透徹，具有金屬質感的明快特質。其音域位處中高音區，發聲時能產生清脆: The khong wong lek's timbre is clear and translucent, bright with a metallic quality. Its range lies in the upper middle register, and when struck it gives a crisp attack with a short ring. Because the gongs are small in diameter the resonating chamber is limited, so the sound dies away quickly, not deep and long like the large gongs. Struck, the timbre has a subtle shimmer and carries well, so it stands out clearly in the ensemble. Compared with the large gong circle the khong wong lek is lighter and more agile; compared with cymbals its timbre is more solid and weighty. Its particular metal lets it join the melodic instruments to the bass instruments in Thai traditional music, an important addition to the rhythmic layer.
小鑼圈（Khong Wong Lek）是泰國古典音樂使用的鑼圈類體鳴樂器，由十八: The Khong Wong Lek is a gong-circle idiophone used in Thai classical music, made up of eighteen tuned bossed gongs, each tuned underneath with beeswax. It is smaller and higher in pitch than the khong wong yai, and the two are played the same way; the khong wong lek usually plays a faster, more ornamented variation of the main melody and uses two-note chords less often. It is the equivalent of Cambodia's Kong toch.
小鑼圈（Khong Wong Lek）為泰國古典音樂中的體鳴鑼圈樂器，由十八個調: The Khong Wong Lek is a gong-circle idiophone of Thai classical music, made up of eighteen tuned bossed gongs. Its origin can be traced to the reign of Rama III (1824–1854), when it was created by skilled musicians. It is played the same way as the khong wong yai but is higher in pitch, taking the faster, more ornamented variation of the main melody and using two-note chords less often. The source also notes that it is the equivalent of Cambodia's Kong toch, which shows its place among the gong circles of Southeast Asia.
手持樂器，以敲擊方式發聲。手持樂器本體，透過敲擊、搖晃、刮奏或撥彈等方式使樂器本: A hand-held instrument that sounds when struck. Hold the body of the instrument and make it vibrate by striking, shaking, scraping or plucking it. Different parts and different amounts of force give different timbres. In practice, first check that you are holding the instrument correctly, and once the basic way of sounding it is secure, work on rhythm patterns and melodies. Strike the surface with a finger or a drumstick and let the rebound carry the hand back naturally, keeping the wrist relaxed.
